Here's the deal. I've been dual booting windows and ubuntu for years. In my ideal world I want to use ubuntu for all things internet and windows for programs I need that aren't compatible with linux. The problem is, ever since I installed unbuntu it has given me nothing but problems in regards to wifi. It would cut out randomly. Hours of googling and trying different commands led me nowhere but I stuck with the OS because I loved it and just assumed I had a shitty wireless card/router/cable modem. Fast forward 3ish years dealing with that crap and here I am with a new laptop, new router and new cable modem and I am STILL having issues with Ubuntu and wifi. It doesn't cut out nearly as much as it used to, and when it does I just have to restart the PC, not the router. But the main problem is, with this new install, I get HORRIBLE speeds. Depends on what WiFi NIC you have. WLAN NIC drivers can be spotty to straight up a pile of shit, depending on the brand. Broadcom, for example, only has proprietary drivers. Issues with their hardware can't be legally addressed by Ubuntu developers, although that won't stop those who like to tinker anyways.

I used to have a router that, for some reason, just didn't play well with linux clients. It was doing something wrong - I don't remember what - which screwed up linux, but not windows. This was back in the days of 802.11b, iirc. Anyway, it's another thing to consider if this has all been happening with the same router.

I too have this problem with Network Manager. Some wifi cards' firmware have problems with Network Manger (I think that's what Ubuntu 14 uses for the default.) You would need to troubleshoot the problem (dmesg after a disconnect, google the error) to see if a patched version of Network Manager might help.

You could alternatively stop or disable the Network Manager service and configure it manually in /etc/network/interfaces (look up the instructions on how it's done for Ubuntu Server) or using wpa_supplicant. (I'm not sure if netctl / wifi-menu is available for Ubuntu 14, which works for me on Arch Linux)

Personally, I find wpa_supplicant easier since it's just a single file and a few commands. For example, the script I use to start wpa_supplicant (with sudo):

#!/bin/bash
# start_wifi.sh

pkill wpa_supplicant
pkill dhclient

ifconfig wlan0 down
ifconfig wlan0 up

wpa_supplicant -Dwext -B -iwlan0 -c/etc/wpa_supplicant.conf
dhclient wlan0

and my /etc/wpa_supplicant.conf looks like this (edited with sudo. the connection uses personal WPA2):

ctrl_interface=/var/run/wpa_supplicant
ctrl_interface_group=root

network={
 ssid="my_home_ssid"
 scan_ssid=1
 key_mgmt=WPA-PSK
 psk="my plain ascii password"
}
I hear your pain, and while I don't have any answers for you, I'm happy to see the overwhelming positive response from the community! What laptop do you have? (Exact model would be useful...)

You would need to construct (or buy) a step-down transformer or a voltage divider. I am assuming you have resistors for the latter. Wikipedia has an example with numbers on it, so you should be able to follow it easily. If you are lacking the required resistance at either of the two nodes R1 or R2, remember you can run resistors in series to achieve the require resistance.

If the power source and device are both DC, you want a linear regulator or a buck converter. Only use a transformer to step down AC to AC.
